column2: **A web session manager stores 700K active sessions in hash table with 1M buckets (load factor α=0.7). System architect proposes reducing table size to 500K buckets (α=1.4) to save memory. What's the performance impact?**
column3: Load factor α = n/m (elements/buckets). For chaining: average search O(1+α). At α=0.7, avg chain length ~0.7 (fast). At α=1.4, avg chain ~1.4 (slower but acceptable). However, higher load increases worst-case clustering. Beyond α=1, open addressing becomes impractical (no free slots). Chaining tolerates α>1, open addressing requires α<1. Trade-off: memory vs performance.
column13: No impact on performance with chaining
column14: Higher load factor increases average chain length; chaining tolerates α>1 but performance degrades
column15: Open addressing works better at α=1.4

column2: **User authentication system hashes passwords. Developer uses simple hash: sum of ASCII values modulo table size. For table size 100, passwords 'abc' (97+98+99=294%100=94) and 'bca' (same sum) collide. What property is violated?**
column3: Good hash function should minimize collisions for similar inputs. Summation is order-independent: 'abc', 'bac', 'cab' all hash identically. This is catastrophic for anagrams. Violates avalanche effect: small input change should drastically change output. Better: polynomial rolling hash h=Σ(char[i] × p^i) mod m where p is prime. This makes order matter. Used in: Rabin-Karp, distributed hashing.
column14: Order-independent summation causes anagram collisions; violates distribution uniformity
column15: Table size too small for load

column2: **Online shopping cart stores items in hash table with chaining (linked lists at each bucket). Table has 1000 buckets, 5000 items. In worst case, what causes O(n) search time?**
column3: Worst case: all elements hash to same bucket, creating single chain of n elements. Search becomes O(n) linear scan. Happens with poor hash function or adversarial input. Example: if hash always returns 0, all 5000 items in bucket 0. Average case O(1+α) assumes uniform distribution. To prevent: use good hash function, cryptographic hashing for adversarial inputs, or universal hashing.
column14: All elements hash to same bucket creating O(n) chain

column2: **Cache system uses open addressing with linear probing: hash(k) = k%10. Inserting sequence [11,21,31,41,12]. After inserting first four (all hash to bucket 1), they occupy buckets 1,2,3,4. Inserting 12 (hashes to 2) causes how many probes?**
column3: 12 hashes to bucket 2, but 1-4 are occupied due to primary clustering. Linear probe sequence: 2→3→4→5. Takes 4 probes to find empty bucket 5. Primary clustering: consecutive filled slots grow, increasing probe length. Formula: probes = 1/(1-α) where α=5/10=0.5, avg ~2 probes. But clustering creates hot spots with worse locality. Quadratic probing reduces clustering.
column14: 4 probes due to primary clustering from consecutive occupied buckets

column2: **Email server uses quadratic probing: probe sequence h(k), h(k)+1², h(k)+2², h(k)+3²,... with table size m=16 (power of 2). For load factor α=0.6 (10 elements), does quadratic probing guarantee finding empty slot?**
column3: Quadratic probing with table size power of 2 guarantees finding slot if α<0.5. Beyond α=0.5, may not probe all positions (only half the table). At α=0.6, may fail to find empty slot even if exists. Solution: use prime table size (guarantees probing all slots if α<1) or double hashing. Theorem: for prime m and α<1, probing sequence visits all buckets.
column14: May fail to find slot; power-of-2 table only guarantees α<0.5

column2: **Social media platform's hash table reaches 75% capacity (α=0.75 threshold). System doubles table size from 1M to 2M buckets and rehashes all entries. What's the time complexity of resize operation?**
column3: Resize requires rehashing all n elements: create new table (2m buckets), compute new hash for each element (hash values change with table size), insert into new table. Time O(n) for n elements. Amortized analysis: if doubling at α=0.75, average insert remains O(1). Frequent small resizes waste time; infrequent large resizes cause latency spikes. Typical: double when α>0.75, halve when α<0.25.

column2: **Distributed cache with 4 servers uses consistent hashing. Servers and keys map to ring [0, 2³²). Server S1 at position 100M, S2 at 500M, S3 at 1.5B, S4 at 3B. Key K hashes to 800M. Which server stores K?**
column3: In consistent hashing ring, key stored on first server clockwise from key's hash position. K=800M: S1(100M) < K < S3(1.5B). Next server clockwise is S3. When server fails (e.g., S3), only keys between S2 and S3 need remapping to S4. Traditional hashing: removing 1 of n servers remaps ~(n-1)/n keys. Consistent hashing: removes ~1/n keys. Used in: distributed caches, load balancers.
column14: S3 stores K as first server clockwise from 800M

column2: **Implementing hash function for strings in hash table. Two approaches: (1) sum ASCII values, (2) polynomial rolling hash Σ(char[i]×31^i). For strings 'listen' and 'silent', which approach avoids collision?**
column3: Approach 1 (sum): 'listen' and 'silent' have same ASCII sum (anagrams), collide. Approach 2 (polynomial): 'l'×31⁰ + 'i'×31¹ + 's'×31² +... ≠ 's'×31⁰ + 'i'×31¹ + 'l'×31² +... (different positions, different powers). Polynomial considers position. Prime base (31) reduces patterns. Java String.hashCode() uses polynomial. Trade-off: polynomial is O(n) for n-char string vs O(n) for sum, but better distribution.
column14: Polynomial rolling hash considers position avoiding anagram collisions
column15: Both approaches have same collision rate

column2: **User database uses linear probing. Sequence: insert 21→bucket 1, insert 31→bucket 2 (collision, probed), delete 21. Later searching for 31 starts at bucket 1 (empty after deletion), stops search, reports not found. What's the solution?**
column3: Lazy deletion: mark deleted slots as 'tombstone' rather than empty. Search continues past tombstones, insert can reuse tombstones. Without tombstones, deletion breaks probe chains causing false negatives. Example: search for 31: bucket 1→tombstone (continue)→bucket 2 (found). Trade-off: tombstones accumulate, degrading performance. Eventually requires table rebuild. Chaining avoids this issue.
column14: Use tombstone markers allowing search continuation
column16: Linear probing doesn't have this issue

column2: **URL blacklist filter uses Bloom filter with 3 hash functions and 1M bits for 100K URLs (10 bits per element). Filter may report URL as 'possibly malicious' (false positive) but never 'safe' when actually malicious (no false negatives). What's the approximate false positive rate?**
column3: Bloom filter false positive rate: (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k where k=hash functions, n=elements, m=bits. For k=3, n=100K, m=1M: ≈(1-e^(-0.3))^3 ≈ 0.0435 (4.35%). As filter fills, FP rate increases. Optimal k = (m/n)×ln(2) ≈ 7 for m/n=10. Never false negatives: if all k bits not set, element definitely absent. Used in: caches, spell checkers, databases.
column14: ~4-5% false positive rate with given parameters

column2: **E-commerce site displays products. HashMap retrieval O(1), TreeMap O(log n). Product listing requires sorted order by ID. Which structure and why?**
column3: HashMap doesn't maintain order: iteration order unpredictable. TreeMap maintains sorted order (Red-Black tree): iteration gives sorted sequence. For sorted requirements, TreeMap despite O(log n) cost. Alternative: HashMap for storage, sort on retrieval O(n log n). Trade-off depends on read/write ratio. High reads: TreeMap better. High writes: HashMap + occasional sort. LinkedHashMap maintains insertion order (not sorted).

column2: **Web server hash table for session IDs uses predictable hash function hash(x)=x%1000. Attacker sends requests with IDs [1000, 2000, 3000, ..., 100000] all hashing to bucket 0. What attack is this and how to prevent?**
column3: Hash collision DoS attack: adversary crafts inputs causing maximum collisions, degrading O(1) to O(n) performance. All 100 requests hash to bucket 0, creating 100-element chain. Prevention: (1) randomized hashing with secret seed (changes per restart), (2) cryptographic hash, (3) limit chain length, (4) switch to balanced tree after threshold. SipHash designed for this. Used in: Python 3.3+, Ruby 1.9+.

column2: **LRU cache stores 1000 items. Operations: get(key), put(key, value). Both must be O(1). Implementation combines hash map for O(1) lookup and what data structure for O(1) LRU ordering?**
column3: Doubly linked list maintains LRU order: head=most recent, tail=least recent. Hash map: key → node pointer in list. get(key): hash lookup O(1), move node to head O(1). put(key): hash lookup O(1), if cache full remove tail O(1), insert at head O(1). Total O(1) for both operations. Single structure can't achieve both. List alone: O(n) search. Hash alone: no ordering.

column2: **Finding substring pattern 'abc' in text 'xyzabcdef' using Rabin-Karp rolling hash. Hash function: h=Σ(char[i]×26^i) mod p. After computing hash for 'xyz', how to compute hash for 'yza' in O(1)?**
column3: Rolling hash: remove leftmost character, shift, add rightmost character. h('xyz') = x×26² + y×26¹ + z×26⁰. To get h('yza'): subtract x×26² (leftmost), multiply remainder by 26 (shift), add a×26⁰ (rightmost). Formula: h_new = (h_old - text[i]×26^(m-1)) × 26 + text[i+m]. O(1) per position vs O(m) recomputation. Enables O(n+m) pattern matching.

column2:
**Finding count of subarrays with sum=k. Array: [1,2,3], k=3. Subarrays: [1,2], [3]. Count=2. Brute force: O(n²) checking all subarrays. What hash-based approach achieves O(n)?**

```python
def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    count = 0
    prefix_sum = 0
    sum_freq = {0: 1}  # Base case: empty subarray
    
    for num in nums:
        prefix_sum += num
        if prefix_sum - k in sum_freq:
            count += sum_freq[prefix_sum - k]
        sum_freq[prefix_sum] = sum_freq.get(prefix_sum, 0) + 1
    
    return count
```

**Why does tracking prefix sum in hash work?**
column3: If subarray [i,j] sums to k, then prefix_sum[j] - prefix_sum[i-1] = k. Rearranged: prefix_sum[i-1] = prefix_sum[j] - k. For each position j, check if (current_prefix - k) seen before. Count tracks frequency for duplicate prefix sums. Example: [1,2,3], k=3. At index 1: prefix=3, (3-3)=0 in hash (count=1). At index 2: prefix=6, (6-3)=3 in hash (count=1). Total=2. Time O(n), Space O(n).
column14: Track prefix sums in hash; check if (current_prefix - k) exists

column2: **Social network finds common friends between two users. User A: 10K friends (set A), User B: 15K friends (set B). Using hash sets, what's the time complexity for finding intersection A∩B?**

column2:
**Grouping anagrams in word list: ['eat','tea','tan','ate','nat','bat']. Result: [['eat','tea','ate'], ['tan','nat'], ['bat']]. What hash key groups anagrams together?**

```python
def group_anagrams(words):
    from collections import defaultdict
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    
    for word in words:
        key = ''.join(sorted(word))  # What makes this work?
        groups[key].append(word)
    
    return list(groups.values())
```

**Why does sorted string work as hash key?**
column3: Anagrams have same letters, different order. Sorted string is canonical form: 'eat'→'aet', 'tea'→'aet', 'ate'→'aet'. Same key → same bucket. Hash groups anagrams automatically. Time O(n×k log k) where n=words, k=avg word length (sorting cost). Alternative: character frequency as key (26-letter array/tuple) O(n×k). Both group anagrams correctly.
column14: Sorted string canonical form groups anagrams with same hash key

column2: **Database index grows from 1M to 2M entries. Two rehashing strategies: (1) double table size immediately when threshold reached, (2) incremental rehashing spreading over many operations. What's the latency trade-off?**
column3: Strategy 1 (immediate): single operation takes O(n) time (all entries rehashed), causes latency spike, but subsequent operations O(1). Strategy 2 (incremental): each operation rehashes few entries, amortizes cost, no spikes, slightly higher average cost per operation. Used in Redis: maintains two hash tables, gradually migrates. For real-time systems (low latency required), incremental better. For batch systems, immediate acceptable.
column14: Immediate causes O(n) spike; incremental amortizes cost avoiding latency spikes

Infeasible for dynamic sets (new keys invalidate function). Used in: compilers, static configuration, minimal perfect hashing for space efficiency.

column2: **Database joins two tables: Customers (1M rows) and Orders (10M rows) on customer_id. Hash join algorithm builds hash table on smaller table (Customers), probes with larger table (Orders). Why hash smaller table?**
column3: Hash smaller table: 1M entries × O(1) insert = O(1M) build phase. Probe with 10M × O(1) lookup = O(10M) probe phase. Total O(11M). If hash larger table: 10M build + 1M probe = O(11M) same asymptotically, but higher constant (10M hash table vs 1M). Memory: hash table size proportional to smaller table. For nested loop join: 1M×10M = O(10¹³) comparisons. Hash join dramatically faster.

column2: **To defend against hash collision attacks, system uses universal hashing: randomly selects hash function from family at runtime. Function family: h_a,b(k) = ((ak + b) mod p) mod m where p is prime > universe size, a,b random. What property does universal hashing guarantee?**
column3: Universal hashing guarantees: for any two distinct keys x≠y, probability of collision Pr[h(x)=h(y)] ≤ 1/m (table size). Over all random choices of h from family. This bound holds regardless of keys (no adversarial input). Expected collisions for any key: ≤ α (load factor). Deterministic hash: adversary crafts n keys all colliding. Universal: adversary cannot predict which function selected.
column14: Collision probability ≤ 1/m for any key pair regardless of adversarial input
column16: Only works with prime table sizes

column2: **File backup system deduplicates 1TB data (1M files) using content-based hashing (SHA-256). Hash collisions for SHA-256 are astronomically rare (2^-256). What's the time and space complexity for detecting duplicates?**
column3: Compute hash for each file: O(file_size) per file. Store in hash set: O(1) per hash. Total time O(Σfile_sizes) = O(total_data) for hashing + O(n) for n files. Space O(n) for n hashes (32 bytes each = 32MB for 1M files). Collision probability negligible: can assume no collisions. Alternative: byte-by-byte comparison O(n²×file_size) infeasible. Content hashing enables O(n) deduplication. Used in: Git, dedup storage, backup systems.
column14: O(total_data) for hashing + O(n) space for hash storage

column2: **MapReduce job processes 1B records across 1000 machines. Records partitioned by hash(key) mod 1000 to assign machines. Key distribution: 80% of keys have hash values 0-99 (skewed). What problem occurs and how to fix?**
column3: Hash partitioning with skewed distribution: machines 0-99 overloaded (800M records), machines 100-999 underloaded (200M records). Causes stragglers, poor parallelism. Fix: (1) use better hash function for uniform distribution, (2) range partitioning if keys have known distribution, (3) consistent hashing with virtual nodes, (4) dynamic load balancing. Uniform hashing critical for distributed systems.
column14: Skewed hash causes load imbalance; need uniform hash or load balancing

column2: **Cuckoo hashing uses two hash functions h₁, h₂ and two tables. Inserting key: if h₁(key) occupied, displace existing, try inserting displaced key at its alternate location (h₂). For tables size 5 each, inserting [1,2,3,4,5,6] with h₁(x)=x%5, h₂(x)=(x+1)%5. What happens inserting 6 after others?**
column3: After inserting 1-5 in table 1 (all buckets full), inserting 6: h₁(6)=1 (occupied by 1), displace 1, try h₂(1)=2 (occupied by 2), displace 2, try h₁(2)=2 (occupied), cycle detected. Rehash with new functions. Cuckoo hashing guarantees O(1) worst-case lookup (check both locations), but insertion can fail requiring rehash. Typically succeeds if α<0.5 per table (total α<1 for both tables).
column14: Displacement chain may cycle requiring rehash with new hash functions

column2: **Embedded system compares data structures: array (100% utilization), hash table with chaining (load factor 0.7, pointer overhead 8 bytes/entry). For storing 1M 32-bit integers, what's approximate memory ratio hash:array?**
column3: Array: 1M × 4 bytes = 4MB. Hash table: 1M/0.7 ≈ 1.43M buckets × 4 bytes (assuming array-based buckets) + 1M × (4 bytes data + 8 bytes pointer) = 5.72MB + 12MB = 17.72MB. Ratio ≈ 4.4:1. Hash provides O(1) access but significant memory overhead. For memory-constrained systems, arrays/sorted arrays better if access patterns allow. Trade-off: speed vs space.

column14: Hash table uses ~4-5x more memory due to buckets and pointers

column2: **Database uses extendible hashing: global depth d, local depths per bucket. Initially d=2, 4 buckets (00,01,10,11). Bucket 01 overflows, splits. What happens to global depth and bucket structure?**
column3: Bucket 01 splits into two: 001 and 011 (local depth 3). If current global depth d=2 insufficient to distinguish, increase global depth to d=3, double directory size to 8 entries. Directory entries 001,011 point to new buckets, others map to existing buckets. Allows dynamic growth without full rehash. Only overflowing bucket splits. Used in: dynamic file systems, databases (ISAM), when avoiding full rehash critical.
column14: Overflow increases local depth; global depth increases if needed doubling directory
